newsitem.title: UK: SWIMMING-NO BRITISH OFFICIAL APPEAL FOR GILLINGHAM.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-NO BRITISH OFFICIAL APPEAL FOR GILLINGHAM.

text.p: The British Olympic Association (BOA) has dropped plans to appeal against a decision to deny swimmer Nick Gillingam a bronze medal after a Russian rival's positive drugs test at the Atlanta Games, a BOA official said on Monday.

Gillingham finished fourth in the 200 metres breaststroke but was promoted to third when Russia's Andrei Korneyev was stripped of his bronze medal by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) after testing positive for the substance bromantan.

But the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld a Russian appeal and overturned the IOC ruling, saying it had not been proved that bromantan was a stimulant to a standard sufficient to justify withdrawing the medal.

Gillingham, at 29 the oldest swimming finalist in Atlanta, would have become the first British swimmer to win a medal at three successive Olympics. He was told at the time he would have the backing of the BOA in any appeal.
But, after legal discussions, the BOA has decided the judgment was "not open to direct challenge" by themselves or any other body.
"I am bitterly disappointed at the decision," Gillingham, who retired after the Games, said. "I believe there should be an appeal and I should have financial support to lodge an appeal.
"The CAS report clearly indicates that at a Games where we were told technology would catch all cheats, the Russians have got away with it by staying one step ahead of the medical code."
Gillingham is considering whether to lodge an appeal of his own but realises the legal costs could be prohibitive.
BOA press officer Pat Ewing said on Monday the association had every sympathy for Gillingham's plight but had taken the decision after discussions with their legal advisers.
"We've told Nick that the decision is just not open to challenge from the BOA, the IOC or himself. We have every sympathy for his position," Ewing said.
"But, in effect, the CAS determined there was insufficient evidence to categorise bromantan as a banned substance."

Korneyev was among five athletes, four Russians and a Lithuanian, who tested positive in Atlanta for bromantan, a psycho-stimulant used by Russian cosmonauts to reduce feelings of fatigue and make the body more tolerant to heat.
